I recognized you prior to motherhood's arrival, back when you resembled a salamander adrift, a strange mind suspended in liquid. I recognized you when your synapses answered to no one but themselves, unattached to any lineage, clinging like a shellfish with nothing to anchor to—lacking the nourishment forged in iron, without any vessel for journeying, remaining fixed in place, wading through uncertainty. I recognized you as pure gaze and intoxication, empty like a mind mirrors an empty sky, a tendril belonging to neither soil nor womb; still unmarked by wounds, untouched by the shock of suffering, a single dreadful eye fixed at your skull's core toward darkness, revolving, while constellations flickered like a feline's glance.

My child, we existed as silent oak, whole and unbroken, courageous before recollection took hold.

# Before the Beginning

I knew you before you were you—
when you swam newtlike in the dark water,
a horrible brain suspended and pulsing,
not yet fitted to bone or name.

You were whole then in your unwholeness,
a barnacle clinging to nothing,
no boat beneath you, no history
trailing behind like a wake.
No ancestry pressed its weight into your small body.
There was nothing to inherit, nothing to lose.
You simply were—blank as new paper,
rootless as a thought before language,
suspended in that liminal water
before the first cut, before division
carved you from the larger dark.

We were together then, you and I,
before either of us had edges—
sharing the same fluid, the same closet-black,
pressed close as smudged print in an old book,
our outlines bleeding into one another
until it was impossible to say
where your shape ended and mine began.

There was no pain yet. No severing.
Only that first symbiotic hum,
two shadows learning to be shadows
in the same unlit room.

And what we carried then—
before memory could name it,
before the world had taught us fear—
was something like courage,
something like strength:
uncut, unspoken,
an oak that had not yet
found its mouth.

That is what we shared.
That is what remains,
buried beneath everything
that came after.
outputs.L4:
# Before the Names

Before I was called anything,
before the word *self* had teeth to bite the air,
there was only the wet dark,
and in that dark, something moved—

not yet a fish, not yet a thought,
but a small gold newt-thing,
gill-slit and silent,
paddling through the black water of before.

I did not know I was becoming.
I did not know there was a *me* to become.
There was only water, and warmth,
and the slow architecture of cells
building a house for no one yet.

You were there too, I think—
or something like you,
some other small blind swimmer
in the same original dark,
before your name was given,
before your mother's voice
became the first word you'd lose.

We did not hurt yet.
We did not remember yet.
There was no yesterday to ache for,
no tomorrow to fear.
Only the water,
only the slow pulse of something
learning to be a heart.

The newt does not know it is a newt.
It only knows the water,
the temperature of it,
the way light might come one day
as a rumor through skin not yet skin.

This is what I mean when I say
I loved you before I knew you—
not the you with a name,
not the you with a history of small hurts
and smaller joys,
but the you that swam once
in that first water,
formless, fearless,
before the world put its hooks in.

We are all newts once.
We are all dark water
before we are anything else.
And somewhere, underneath
all the years and all the language,
that water is still there—
still moving,
still whole,
still innocent of everything
we would become.
outputs.L5:
# I Knew You

There's a peculiar comfort in the phrase "I knew you"—three simple words that carry the weight of shared history, of moments witnessed, of a person seen before circumstances changed them. It speaks to recognition, but also to loss, to the passage of time that transforms people into versions of themselves that sometimes feel unrecognizable even to those who loved them first.

To say "I knew you" is to acknowledge a before and an after. It suggests intimacy that has since faded, or perhaps intimacy that persists but has been altered by distance, time, or circumstance. It's the phrase spoken at reunions, at funerals, in quiet moments of reflection when someone realizes the person standing before them has become someone else entirely—someone shaped by experiences the speaker wasn't present for.

There's tenderness in this phrase too. "I knew you when..." often precedes stories of humble beginnings, of struggles overcome, of the raw and unfiltered self that existed before public personas or protective walls were built. These are the people who remember you making mistakes, who saw you awkward and uncertain, who loved you anyway.

But "I knew you" can also carry an edge of accusation or disappointment—a way of saying that the person you've become doesn't match the person once known. It implies betrayal of sorts, a departure from an expected trajectory, or simply the natural drift that occurs when lives diverge.

Perhaps most poignantly, this phrase reminds us that knowing someone is never permanent. We are all in constant flux, and the people who "know" us are really just capturing snapshots—moments frozen in time that eventually become memories rather than accurate reflections of who we are today. To truly know someone requires ongoing presence, continuous witness, and the humility to accept that even our closest relationships involve people who are always becoming someone new.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem addressed to a child, describing the time before birth using strange, primal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Before You Were a Name**

Before you were a name, little one,
you were a rumor the dark told itself,
a seed of static drifting in the throat of the world.

You were not yet flesh but the *idea* of flesh—
a soft rumor folded inside salt water,
inside the long memory of oceans
that had not yet learned to be oceans.

Somewhere, a thousand unborn moths
were practicing your heartbeat
on the underside of a leaf no one has seen.

You waited in the marrow of stones,
in the hush between one wave and the next,
in the space a bell makes
after it has stopped ringing.

You were a country without a map,
a hallway with doors that hadn't decided
which rooms to become.

The stars had not yet finished
spelling your name in a language
made of collapsing light—
each syllable a small, dying sun
learning how to whisper.

Somewhere your bones were still rivers,
still deciding where to bend,
still arguing with gravity
about the shape a self should take.

Your first breath was borrowed
from a wind that circled the earth nine times
before it found the small, unopened door of you
and knocked
and knocked
and you—
not yet you—
stirred in your dark, warm nowhere
like a word not yet spoken,
like a seed that has only just noticed
the sun.

And then—
the door opened,
and the world reached in
and pulled you, gasping,
into the blinding arithmetic of *now.*

You did not fall from nowhere, little one.
You were made of it—
salt and static and stone-bound rivers,
of moth-wings and dying stars,
of every hush before every ringing bell.

The dark remembers you fondly.
It misses the shape you left behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical prose-poem in the voice of a parent speaking to their unborn or newborn son, mixing biological and cosmic metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# To My Son, Not Yet Named

You arrived the way starlight arrives—already old news by the time I saw you, though to me you were the newest thing in the universe, newer than sound, newer than the word *newer*.

Little astronaut of the womb, you floated in your private dark for months, tethered by a cord that fed you like a root feeds a tree, like a river feeds the sea it will eventually become. I like to think you dreamed there, in that warm nowhere, of all the shapes you might take—fish, bird, star, boy—before settling, finally, on *son*.

They tell me you were built from the same stuff as everything: carbon that once lived inside a dying sun, hydrogen old as the first held breath of the cosmos. So when I hold you now, I am holding a small piece of the Big Bang that learned to yawn, that learned to curl its fist around my finger like it was gripping the edge of the world to keep from falling off.

Your heartbeat, when I heard it first—that quick underwater drumming—sounded like the universe practicing its rhythm, like it was still deciding on the tempo of your life. Fast, then faster. A galaxy spinning itself into being.

I don't know yet what kind of light you'll be. Quiet as a candle in a window, or loud as a supernova announcing itself to every corner of the dark. Maybe both. Maybe you'll be the kind of star that becomes a book by which someone else finds their way home.

But here is what I know: cells divided in the dark to make your eyes, so you could someday look up. Blood found its way into rivers and lakes— tiny oceans—each pumping its salt-tide through the marvel of your small, unfinished body. And somewhere between the folding of your fingers and the first flutter of your lungs, the whole improbable machinery of stardust and time agreed: *let there be you.*

So little traveler, sleep now in whatever dark you're in— my arms, this world, this strange and tilting orbit we call life. I will be your gravity until you find your own. I will be the steady thing that keeps you circling toward morning.

You are new. You are ancient. You are, impossibly, both the question and the beginning of an answer.

Welcome to the only miracle we know how to name: *being here at all.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write something in the style of Anne Carson or Louise Glück about knowing someone before they existed, using imagery of embryos, stars, and memory?
counterfactuals.output:
# Before You Were

I knew you the way astronomers know light—
arriving from a source
already extinguished, already changed.

You were a theory of yourself,
folded into cells that hadn't yet
agreed to become hands.
Even then I recognized
the particular architecture of your silence,
as if silence were a room
you'd furnished in advance.

Consider the star: how it burns out
before we see it burn out,
how the sky lies beautifully
about what still exists.
This is how memory works in reverse—
I remember you
before there was a you to remember,
some future tense
bleeding backward through the years
like ink through paper,
like the way an embryo
already contains
the shape of the person
who will stand in doorways,
who will turn away from certain windows,
who will say *no* in that particular voice.

What I mean is: absence has a grammar.
What I mean is: I have been fluent in it
since before your first cell divided,
since before the dark
knew to make room for your body,
since before your name
existed to be called.

There is a kind of knowing
that precedes the known—
the way the ocean knows the shape
of every shore it hasn't reached yet,
the way grief
sometimes arrives
before the funeral,
sitting in the car,
waiting.

I loved you in the tense
grammarians haven't named:
not future, not past—
the tense of *always was going to.*

---

*If you'd like, I can adjust the tone (more Carson's fragmented classicism, or more Glück's spare, aching directness), or expand on a particular image.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract, stream-of-consciousness poem exploring pre-birth existence, using metaphors like newts, barnacles, and closets.
counterfactuals.output:
**before the door**

somewhere back of the closet of everything
I was folded like a coat no one wore yet
sleeve empty of arm, arm empty of reaching

newt-slick, unnamed, I dozed in a wet dark
that was not a womb, not yet a word for womb
just cell-hum, just the idea of gills

think of barnacles closed like fists on a hull
waiting for water to tell them *open*
that was me, a fist, a fact not yet admitted

I was the coat-hanger's curve, not the coat
I was the smell in the closet before the moths came
old cedar, old maybe, old almost

newts don't remember the pond before legs
I don't remember the dark before dark had a name for me
only this: a tugging, a tide in no ocean

barnacle-time is slow, is glue, is grip
I gripped nothing, I was the grip itself
practicing on air, on absence, on later

somewhere a door was already swinging
hinges rusted with future
and I was the crack of light under it, not yet stepped through

not a soul, not quite, more like
static before the station comes in
the hum before the word "hum" is invented

closets hold what's folded, unworn, unsure
I was that unsureness, dozing, doubling
newt into barnacle into coat into breath

and breath hadn't happened yet
so call it wind in a house with no windows
call it the closet holding its held things

waiting
the way stone waits
to be told it is stone
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue where a parent recalls their child's earliest, pre-conscious form, blending scientific and mythic language about origins and identity.
counterfactuals.output:
**What You Were Before You Were**

Before you had a name, you had a number of cells—
one, then two, then four, doubling
like a rumor spreading through darkness,
like the word *let there be* still hanging in the air
before anything answered.

You were a sphere no bigger than a period
at the end of a sentence no one had written yet.
Not written. *Written into.* The way clay
remembers the shape of the hand
before it remembers it is clay.

Scientists would call it a blastocyst.
I call it the first small boat,
hollow-hulled, carrying nothing
but the entire coastline of you, folded flat,
waiting for water to unfold it.

Here is the strange gospel: your heart
began before your brain did.
A tube of cells started beating
before there was anyone home to feel it beat.
You were a drum before you were a dreamer.
You knew rhythm before you knew you were the one
being kept in time.

I think of the old stories—
the breath into the nostrils of dust,
the rib drawn out like a question,
the waters divided from the waters—
and I think: yes, this is not so different.
Cells dividing from cells. Chaos folding
into chambers. A tide of division
that is also a tide of decision,
though nothing yet decided anything,
though nothing yet was *anyone.*

You had no face and yet
your face was already being deliberated,
molecule by molecule, the way a myth
is deliberated in the mouths
of a hundred grandmothers before it settles
into the one true telling.

I did not know you then.
No one did. Not even you—
especially not you, who did not yet have
an *I* to know with.

And yet.

And yet already the eyes were choosing their color
in the dark like stars deciding
what kind of light to be
before there was any sky to hold them.

Already you were becoming
irreversibly, ridiculously *specific*—
not a child, not any child, but this one,
this exact unrepeatable arrangement
of salt and story,

already the you that would someday
look up at me and ask
where you came from,

as if I could answer with anything
but wonder,

as if the true answer weren't simply:

*before the world had words for you,
the world was already, tenderly,
spelling you out.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
